opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest thing people underweight is the mismatch between what the student sees during training and what it actually generates at inference time. The default recipe is to have the teacher produce a bunch of outputs and fine-tune the student on them. That's simple and often a good starting point, but the student never learns what to do when it makes its own mistakes. At test time it goes slightly off-distribution, and it compounds from there.

So the first question I'd ask is: can you afford to train on the student's own samples? If you can let the student generate and have the teacher give feedback on those trajectories, token-level probabilities or some score, you usually get a much more robust student. It's the same intuition as imitation learning in RL: learn from the states you'll actually visit, not just the expert's states.

The second thing is the objective. Forward KL makes the student cover everything the teacher might say, which can be a problem when the student is much smaller and can't represent all of that. It ends up spreading mass and producing mushy outputs. Reverse KL, or something in between, lets the student commit to the modes it can actually capture. Which one is right depends on the task. For open-ended generation you might want diversity, and for reasoning or tasks with one right answer you often want the student to be sharp and confident.

Third is the capacity gap. A bigger, better teacher isn't automatically a better teacher. If the gap is huge, the student can struggle to imitate it, and sometimes a mid-sized teacher, or a staged setup, works better.

And then there's the practical side: what do you have access to? If you only have API outputs and no logits, your options shrink a lot. If you have full teacher logits and a compute budget for on-policy sampling, you can do much more.

So my short answer: match the training distribution to inference, pick the divergence that fits the task and the student's capacity, and be honest about what teacher signal you can actually get.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The thing I keep coming back to is that distillation is really about the data you generate, not the loss function. People spend a lot of time debating logit matching versus sequence-level KL, but in practice the biggest lever is where the training sequences come from.

The classic recipe is: sample a bunch of outputs from the big teacher, filter them, and fine-tune the student on them. That works, but it has a subtle problem. The student is only ever trained on the teacher's distribution, so at inference time, when it starts making its own kind of mistakes and drifts into states the teacher never showed it, it has no idea how to recover. That's the same exposure bias story people have known about since sequence models existed, and it just gets worse the bigger the gap between teacher and student.

So the first thing I'd say matters is: let the student generate its own samples, and have the teacher provide the signal on those. On-policy distillation. You're correcting the student in the places it actually ends up, rather than in the places the teacher would have ended up. In our experience that gives you a consistent win over just training on teacher outputs, and it's especially noticeable on reasoning tasks where the trajectories are long and errors compound.

The second thing is the choice of divergence, which interacts with the first point. Forward KL, the standard one, makes the student try to cover everything the teacher does. If the student is much smaller it can't, so you get mode averaging, this mushy middle. Reverse KL or something like a Jensen-Shannon lets the student commit to the modes it can actually represent. Once you're sampling from the student, reverse KL becomes very natural to optimize, so those two choices go together.

Third, and this is the boring practical one, is the quality and difficulty mix of the prompts. You want prompts where the teacher is reliably better than the student, otherwise you're paying teacher compute to teach nothing. And you want enough coverage of hard cases that you're not just distilling the easy behavior.

And then I'd say think about what you actually want the student for. If it's a specific capability like math or code, you can be fairly aggressive and task-focused. If it's a general model, you have to worry about losing things the teacher never explicitly demonstrated, and that's where mixing in some of the original pretraining or SFT data matters.

So, short version: get the student in the loop generating data, pick a divergence that matches the capacity gap, and be deliberate about the prompt distribution. The architecture of the student matters far less than people think once those are right.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important thing is being clear about what you want the student model to do. Are you trying to preserve the teacher’s capabilities broadly, or get a smaller model that’s really good at a particular task? That determines what data you use, what signal you distill, and how you measure success.

Then I’d focus on the gap between the examples you train on and what the student encounters when it actually runs. A student can learn to imitate a teacher’s answers on a fixed dataset and still struggle with its own mistakes. So I’d choose the process based on performance under realistic use, given your training and inference budget, rather than just how closely it matches the teacher during training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most important thing is to work backward from what you want the student model to do. Are you trying to preserve broad capabilities, or make it really good at a particular task? And what are your constraints around inference cost and latency?

That determines the data you need and the kind of supervision you want from the teacher. A stronger teacher doesn’t automatically give you a better student—the examples have to be useful and learnable at the student’s capacity. So I’d prioritize the training data and a reliable evaluation loop, then choose the distillation process based on what actually improves the student.
